title: Is nuclear power part of the answer?

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: They're extending the two old reactors by another decade rather than building anything new. Which tells you something.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: It tells you new build is expensive. It doesn't tell you it's wrong.

turns.speaker: Felix
turns.text: It's not just expensive, it's late. Every one of the recent European projects came in years behind and billions over. That's not bad luck three times running, that's the technology.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Or it's having built nothing for thirty years and losing everyone who knew how.

turns.speaker: Felix
turns.text: Possibly. South Korea did build them on time and on budget, to be fair.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: The reason I keep coming back to it is that wind and solar need something underneath them. On a still, dark February week you need power that doesn't care about the weather.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: Storage for a week, for a whole country. That's not a battery problem, that's a different civilisation.

turns.speaker: Felix
turns.text: Gas does that job today and nobody pretends it's clean, so the honest comparison isn't nuclear against renewables. It's nuclear against gas.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: That reframing helps me, actually. I'd been comparing it to the wrong thing.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: The waste still bothers me, mind you. Not technically. Politically. Somebody has to keep a promise for ten thousand years.

turns.speaker: Felix
turns.text: Finland's building exactly that and it's the least discussed part of the whole debate.

turns.speaker: Saira
turns.text: Which is probably because nobody can picture ten thousand years.

points: Two old reactors are being extended rather than replaced with new build.
Felix argues recent European projects were consistently years late and billions over budget, suggesting a problem with the technology rather than bad luck.
Saira counters that the delays reflect lost expertise after thirty years without building; Felix concedes South Korea delivered on time and budget.
Owen's case is that wind and solar need firm backup for still, dark periods, and week-long national storage is not a battery problem.
Felix reframes the comparison as nuclear against gas rather than nuclear against renewables, which Saira accepts.
Owen's remaining objection to waste is political rather than technical: it requires a promise kept for ten thousand years.
